analysis.one_liner: Limits bank overdraft fees and bans fees on most debit card and ATM overdrafts.
analysis.headline: A bill to cap overdraft fees and ban them on most debit card and ATM transactions died in the Senate Banking Committee without a single hearing, vote, or floor action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would sharply limit overdraft fees, the charges banks collect when a customer spends more than is in the account. It would ban overdraft fees on ATM withdrawals and one-time debit card purchases, cap fees for checks and automatic bill payments at one per month and six per year, require any remaining fee to be proportional to the bank's actual cost, and stop banks from reporting paid overdrafts to credit bureaus. It also required the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau to write enforcement rules and froze overdraft fee increases for one year after enactment.
analysis.who_benefits: Bank customers who overdraw their accounts — the bill's own findings say these fees fall hardest on low- and moderate-income people [S3]. They would keep more of their money: no fees on ATM or one-time debit overdrafts, at most one fee per month and six per year for checks and recurring payments, clearer disclosure of fees in marketing and on statements, same-day notice when an account goes negative, transactions posted in the order that minimizes fees, and no negative credit report for overdrafts that are repaid [S2] [S3]. Customers who don't sign up for overdraft coverage could not be given worse account terms than those who do [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Bank customers who overdraw, especially low-income

how_it_helps.text: Bans overdraft coverage fees entirely on ATM transactions and one-time debit card purchases, and bans nonsufficient-fund fees on those same transactions — ending the common pattern of paying a $30-plus fee to cover a small debit purchase [S2] [S3].

Caps overdraft fees for checks and automatic recurring payments at one per calendar month and six per calendar year, and requires any such fee to be reasonable and proportional to the bank's actual cost of covering the transaction [S2] [S3].

Requires banks to disclose overdraft fees in all marketing, show them on monthly statements, notify customers the same day an account goes negative, post transactions in the order that minimizes fees, and exclude overdraft 'available funds' from the displayed balance [S2] [S3].

Prohibits fees when an overdraft results only from a debit hold larger than the actual purchase amount, and bars banks from reporting negative information to credit bureaus for overdrafts that were repaid — including requiring deletion of previously reported negative information [S2] [S3].

Gives the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau two years to write implementing rules, freezes overdraft fee increases for one year after enactment, and guarantees that customers who decline overdraft coverage get accounts on the same terms as everyone else [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Banks and credit unions, which would lose the fee revenue from overdraft and nonsufficient-fund charges — a major earner, since per the bill's findings institutions charge high flat fees per transaction, multiple fees per day, and daily fees on overdrawn accounts [S3]. Some institutions could shift costs elsewhere through other fees or account terms.
analysis.who_pays_short: Banks and credit unions earning overdraft fees

drawbacks.text: Banks could simply stop covering overdrafts on debit and ATM transactions rather than cover them for free, meaning a customer's card would be declined — possibly triggering a merchant returned-payment fee instead of a bank fee [S3].
Fees would remain legal for checks and automatic recurring payments up to the monthly and annual caps, so customers who rely on auto-pay could still be charged [S3].

Banks and credit unions argue overdraft fees cover the cost and risk of advancing money to customers on short notice; eliminating that revenue could lead institutions to raise other fees or trim free account features to compensate.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers who overdraw, the protections are substantial: hard caps, cost-based fees, disclosure, and credit-report cleanup directly attack the practices the bill's own findings describe as piling fees on low- and moderate-income customers [S3]. The main cost falls on bank fee revenue, not on other consumers, though the risk that banks respond by declining more transactions rather than covering them for free is real — a customer protected from a bank fee could instead face a declined card or a merchant charge. On balance the design is consumer-protective, but it never advanced far enough for these tradeoffs to be tested in committee.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate referred the bill to its Banking Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it expired when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Cory Booker introduced the bill on May 22, 2019, with Sen. Sherrod Brown as the original co-sponsor; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee that same day [S3] [S5].
Only one senator signed on as a co-sponsor, and the Banking Committee took no recorded action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — during the entire Congress [S4] [S5].
The bill died in committee when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, without ever reaching the Senate floor [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks and credit unions that collect overdraft and nonsufficient-fund fees are better off; customers who overdraw their accounts continue paying fees under the pre-existing rules.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never came to a vote, so no voting split exists; its only recorded supporters were two Senate Democrats, and the committee where it died had a Republican chair and majority.

industries.note: The bill directly cuts overdraft and nonsufficient-fund fee revenue by banning fees on ATM and one-time debit overdrafts and capping the rest at one per month and six per year, with fees tied to the bank's actual cost [S2] [S3]. The bill's findings describe banks aggressively steering customers into the most expensive flat-fee option and stacking multiple fees per day — revenue that comes straight out of customers' negative balances [S3].

industries.industry: Credit unions and other depository institutions
industries.note: The bill's definition of depository institution covers the full range of institutions under the Federal Reserve Act, so credit unions would lose overdraft fee revenue too [S3]. Many credit unions present coverage as a member service rather than a profit center, which softens the fit, but the fee limits apply to them equally.
